Introduction
P ersonality style is the essence of who you are and how
 you approach life. Knowing your personality style pro-
 vides useful insight into how you communicate, lead others,
 work in teams, and a host of other interactions. Your person-
 ality style is the foundation for what’s commonly referred to
 as “people skills.”
Personality styles are based on the blending of your assertive
 and expressive behavior. These behaviors occur in patterns
 over time and across situations. Use these insights to increase
 your personal effectiveness and enrich working with others.
About This Book
Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition, provides
 an overview of the four personality styles and then examines
 how these styles affect how you behave in a variety of work-
 place situations. Use this book as a guide to learn about the
 four personality styles and how these styles work in coaching,
 leading, communicating, selling, teaming, time management,
 and learning.
HRDQ has devoted considerable research and resources to
 this topic, and it is this body of work that provides the foun-
 dation for the chapters in this book. Throughout, I reference
 the HRDQ Style Model to introduce and illustrate the charac-
 teristics, benefits, and potential trouble spots associated with
 each style.

f you observe people, you may notice that certain pre-
dictable patterns and tendencies exist in their behaviors.
 These patterns enable you to have some degree of certainty
 in how people may behave as you interact with them. And as
 you may know, if it’s true of “them,” it’s true of you.
These patterns of behavior in people are called personality. In
 this chapter, you discover the roots of personality type, the
 role of expressiveness and assertiveness in formulating your
 personality style, and the basics of the four personality style
 patterns.
Familiarizing Yourself with the
 Basics of Personality Style
Personality has been a subject of interest from the very begin-
 nings of civilization. The earliest notions of personality sug-
 gested that individuals were born with ways of being in the
 world (Navajo). The Greek physician Hippocrates (460-370
 BC) codified these “ways of being” into a medical theory
 based on temperaments — certain innate human moods,
 emotions, and behaviors. Modern psychology has provided
 numerous other empirically framed theories of personality.
6 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
Carl Gustav Jung and William Moulton Marston are among the
 most widely known of the psychologists who’ve increased the
 understanding of personality. Jung’s ideas formed the basis of
 the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator assessment, while Marston
 was responsible for developing the DISC model.
Current theories are grouped into the following categories:
vr Psychodynamic
vr‘ Behavioral
vw Situation or social driven patterns
vv Existential (or patterns to make meaning of life)
As you may imagine, plenty of researchers and writers have
 talked about these points of view, which are rich and complex
 theories. Many of the theories address two core qualities of
 personality:
vr Sources within the person that drive efforts to control or
 be part of his environment (degrees of assertiveness)
vr How much social connection or engagement individuals
 typically display (degrees of expressiveness)
Depending on your take of the qualities and how they blend, a
 host of models exist to give greater refinements to these twin
 dimensions of personality.
Observers and researchers of personality also have explored
 the roles of family history, genetic traits, and learning in the
 development of typical personality patterns and not so typical
 patterns — or what’s categorized as dysfunctional personalities.
 For example, everyone is motivated by self-interest, but the nar-
 cissist goes too far in self-promotion and self-indulgence.
Do a web search on personality and personality styles. You
 can access thorough information on all the theories of per-
 sonality and how they were developed. A deeper look into the
 roots of personality gives you an appreciation for the different
 ways of seeing personality patterns.
The current theories are accessible and interesting but not
 as helpful in the day-to-day interactions as simply asking,
 “Whatever the underlying source, what can I see that helps
Chapter 1: Defining Personality Style 7
me understand my interactions with others consistently over
 time?” Personality style is a way of approaching personality
 patterns without delving into other psychological issues.
By paying attention to style, you can efficiently and effectively
 achieve three things:
1. Quickly identify patterns in yourself and others.
2. Link style to important life experiences, such as learn-
 ing, coaching, and leading.
3. Flex the aspects of behavior that are more effective in
 dealing with others.
Knowing What Makes Up a Style
You have a preferred personality style that developed over time.
 Your style reflects how you like to work — alone or with others —
 how you spend your time — talking or reading — and how you
 deal with and share information. Your style is essentially the way
 you act when you're able to do things your own way.
Your preferred style is likely to be used most of the time —
 that’s why it’s “preferred”; however, you may decide to
 behave differently from your style from time to time. You're
 likely to be more effective when you capitalize on the benefits
 of your style and also flex or adapt your style to account for
 the style of the person with whom you wish to interact.
Your style is determined by the degree of assertiveness and
 expressiveness you demonstrate. Assertiveness is essentially
 the effort that you make to influence or control the thoughts
 and actions of others. Expressiveness is the effort you make to
 control emotions and feelings when relating to others.

Checking Out the Four
 Personality Styles
Your style affects how you sell, coach, influence, manage time,
 lead, and learn; it even helps you engage in relationships and
 identify a career choice. While your style doesn’t predict your
 behavior or your choices, it gives you a handle on behavior in
 pragmatic ways and provides you with a foundation of under-
 standing for how you tend to operate.
Getting acquainted with your own style has the added benetfit
 of helping you identify the styles of those around you. By
 understanding the elements of personality style, you have a
 greater chance at building and maintaining the relationships
 and connections that matter in your life. In this section, I
 cover the different personality types, so maybe you can start
 to see which type you are. For a deeper discussion of the per-
 sonality types, see Chapter 2.
If you read the preceding section and completed your ratings,
 you can see that four relative patterns emerge, illustrated in
 Figure 1-2.
On the HRDQ style model, your behaviors fall into four differ-
 ent quadrants:
vr Top left-hand quadrant: High assertive and low expres-
 sive behaviors fall into this quadrant. If you happen to
 land here, you may show your style by telling others
 information, and you're able to control emotions. This
 pattern usually results in an individual having a Direct
 Style.
» Top right-hand quadrant: This quadrant contains the
 high assertive and high expressive behaviors, which are
 typically demonstrated by telling others information and
 displaying your emotions. This pattern results in an indi-
 vidual having a Spirited Style.
vr Bottom left-hand quadrant: If you fall in this quadrant,
 you show low assertive and low expressive behaviors.
 You demonstrate these qualities by asking others for
 information and controlling emotions. This pattern usu-
 ally results in an individual having a Systematic Style.

(Gene acquainted with your own style helps you in
 many areas of your life. Knowing your style affects
how you sell, coach, influence, manage time, lead, and learn.
 It can even help you in your relationships and your career

In this chapter, you discover the ins and outs of each style:

Looking at the Elements
 of the Direct Style
If you have the tendency to say that you know what needs
 to be done, when it needs to be done, and how it should be
 done, then you're using a Direct Style. This style demon-
 strates a very straightforward and decisive approach during
14 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
interactions. Generally, individuals with this style seem tough
 minded, are focused on what needs to get done, and prefer to
 complete tasks quickly.
The Direct Style is based on being assertive and controlled
 in expressing your emotions. Direct Style is high on assertive
 and low on expressive behaviors. For more on where this
 style lands on the style continuum, see Chapter 1.
Direct Style has the following characteristics:
vr Take charge
vw Get results — now!
vr Compete with vigor
vw Organize tasks for practical outcomes
 vr Pursue risks confidently
Individuals of the Direct Style walk fast, speak fast, and assert
 control.
Noticing the trouble spots
 of the Direct Style
All styles bring benefits and potential trouble spots. The trou-
 ble spots can begin to outweigh the perceived value of the
 style unless the individual learns how to moderate the style
 and flex.
Flexing your style means adjusting your instinctual behavior
 to achieve the desired result. If you don’t flex, you're likely
 to experience frustration and disappointment in many situa-
 tions, as will those around you. See the section “Making the
 Direct Style flex” for more information.
The Direct Style isn’t without trouble spots. Often those who
 prefer the Direct Style are unaware that their behaviors trig-
 ger reactions that can create problems. Some of the trouble
 spots include the following:
vr Being perceived as a poor listener
vr Appearing impatient and terse with others
Chapter 2: Deciphering Your Personality Style 7 5
= WM” Arguing without being open to new information or ideas
 vr Competing at all costs
vr Discounting others’ feelings, reactions, and perceptions
vr Showing disinterest in collaboration
Making the Direct Style flex
Flexing the Direct Style has two avenues: reducing the degree
 of assertiveness and increasing emotional expressions of
 warmth and regard. The Direct Style is useful in situations
 when you need to:
wv Get to the bottom line quickly
vr Speak forcefully (as in preventing an accident)
. V Assert control to communicate authority and direction
Those with the Direct Style need to calibrate how much asser-
 tive behavior is appropriate and how much emotional energy
 to show in certain situations. For example, demonstrating a
 Direct Style while dealing with an immediate crisis works very
 well, but it may not be as effective when dealing with change
 when people’s emotional needs may need to be considered.

Identifying the trouble spots
The Spirited Style has some challenging areas, as well. Some

vr Being perceived as overly dramatic

Flexing the Spirited Style
Flexing the Spirited Style requires you to rein in your asser-
 tive or expressive behaviors in some situations. Because
the Spirited Style uses high degrees of both assertive and
 expressive behaviors, it’s important to read the situations and
 people you're dealing with to see if you may need to tone it
 down a little. The Spirited Style is useful in situations where
 you need to
vr Generate enthusiasm about ideas and possibilities
vr Inspire commitment to key goals and visions
vw Strengthen alliances to keep everyone working in the
 same direction
vr Rally support for pursuing key objectives
Those with the Spirited Style should adjust how much asser-
 tive behavior is appropriate and how much emotional energy
 to exhibit, depending on their surroundings. For example,
 demonstrating a Spirited Style while making a presentation
 to introduce an exciting new product works very well, but
 this style may not work so well when the negative results of a
 health and safety audit need to be explained.

Sifting through the
 Systematic Style
Careful planning and thorough organization in your approach
 to getting things done are the key elements of the Systematic
 Style. This style pays close attention to details, efficiency,
 and careful problem-solving. Generally, individuals with this
 style seem very focused on priorities and make sure to follow
 guidelines or standard operating procedures.
The Systematic Style is based on being more focused on inter-
 nal awareness than externally asserting ideas or information
 and controlling emotions. The Systematic Style is the result of
 low assertive and low emotionally expressive behaviors. For
 more on where this style lands on the style continuum, see
 Chapter 1.
The Systematic Style has the following characteristics:
Wr Follows the guidelines and standard procedures
 vr Gets results by working efficiently
 vr Organizes details, steps, and processes
vr Makes decisions using verified facts and reliable methods
vr Pursues high standards through careful analysis
Spotting the trouble areas
The Systematic Style brings about certain challenges. Often
 those who prefer the Systematic Style are unaware that their
 behavior triggers reactions that can create problems.
Some of the trouble spots include the following:
vr Being perceived as impersonal and cold
 vr Appearing disinterested in interacting with others
vr Seeming overly reliant on tried-and-true procedures at
 the cost of new ideas and innovation
vw Failing to build collaborative relationships

Knowing how to flex the
 Systematic Style
If you fall into the Systematic Style category, make sure to
 pay attention to when you need to elevate assertive behavior
 and how much emotional energy to show when working with
 others. The Systematic Style is useful in situations when you
 need to
vr Make sure a thorough, analytical approach is provided
vw Rely on controlled, methodical decision-making
vr Use a well-organized and efficient problem-solving
. approach
Flexing the Systematic Style has two avenues: increasing the
 degree of being assertive and increasing emotional expres-
 sions of warmth and regard. For example, demonstrating a
 Systematic Style while implementing a business plan works
 very well, but it may not work so well when dealing with activ-
 ities to boost team enthusiasm and commitment.
Comprehending the
 Considerate Style
Do you have the desire to know what everyone else is think-
 ing, and do you seek to build relationships by being friendly
 and accommodating? If so, you've landed yourself in the
 Considerate Style. This style demonstrates a high emotional
 expressiveness and very little assertiveness. If you display
 this style, you typically are thoughtful, trusting, caring, and
 supportive of others.
The benefits of the Considerate Style are numerous.
 Individuals who prefer this style often demonstrate a keen
 interest in working with others and building relationships.
 Individuals with this style like to work with others to get
 things done.
The Considerate Style has the following characteristics:

vw Listens to others
vr Gets results through teams
 vr Collaborates and values relationships
 vr Supports others
vw Prefers a gentle, “steady as you go” approach

 of the Considerate Style
People who fall into the Considerate Style may have a few
 issues. Some of these include the following:
WING!

 vr Unwilling to express opinions for fear of offending others
 vr Telling others what they want to hear
vr Showing little interest in facts, analysis, and debate
Managing your style
Those with the Considerate Style need to consider the
 amount of assertive behavior that is appropriate and how
 much emotional energy to show in a presenting situation. For
 example, demonstrating a Considerate Style while seeking to
 initiate open sharing or discussions with a team is likely to be

The Considerate Style is useful in situations when you need to
=” Strengthen team relationships
vr Address the personal needs of others
. V Coach others with supportive and caring language
Flexing the Considerate Style includes increasing your
 degree of assertiveness and decreasing your emotional

Chapter 3
Applying the Four Styles
 In Communication
( ommunicating means that you're trying to get your
 ideas, perceptions, or explanations understood the way
you intended. You're likely to feel that communication was
 “clear” when the meaning of what was said is mutually under-
 stood. You achieve this understanding through several dimen-
 sions of communicating.
Interestingly, communication involves more than the words
 you use. Some experts argue that up to 70 percent of the
 meaning people take from your efforts to communicate come
 from your paraverbal (voice tone) and nonverbal behaviors
 (facial expressions and body language). Your paraverbal
 behavior — the way you say what you want to share — is cen-
 tral to getting your message across. Your body language —
 nonverbal behavior — covers everything from how you shake
 hands to facial expressions and is part of your communication
 style.
Your communication style is the product of the mixture of your
 assertiveness and emotional expressiveness that makes your
 personality style, which is blended with all of the other aspects
 of communication. In other words, each style has general
 patterns in paraverbals and nonverbals, which are important
 to understand.
22 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
After you've decided the message you want to give to an indi-
 vidual or to a group, you need to attend to the basic elements
 of communicating a message:
vw Establishing a connection with the audience of one or
 one thousand, making sure that the reason for the com-
 munication is clear
vw Creating a common understanding of the message being
 delivered and received
vw Facilitating the exploration of the implications of the
 communication
vr Wrapping up the message and verifying common
 understanding
As you engage in each of these elements of communicating,
 the use of your personality style reveals your communica-
 tion style. Importantly, learning to flex your personality style
 enhances your communication effectiveness as you engage
 with others through each element of communication.
All communication styles can be equally effective. Also, com-
 munication styles that don’t match the needs of the audience
 or receiver of the communication can result in a failed com-
 munication. You need to understand the benefits and poten-
 tial challenges each style tends to demonstrate, inclusive of
 paraverbal and nonverbal behavior.
Communication is complex. You have to consider the mes-
 sage that your words, tone, and body language give to your
 audience. All of it is magnified by your personality style.
The Ins and Outs of the
 Four Personality Styles
 in Communication
Communication tactics are a direct result of your personality
 style. In this section, you review the four personality styles in
 communication and see how each style provides a useful way
 to get your message across. You also discover the potential
Chapter 3: Applying the Four Styles in Communication 23
challenges you may encounter with your style if you don’t
 learn to flex it in communication.
Direct Style
The Direct Style works best when the audience or recipient
 of the message needs direction and responds well to asser-
 tive and low expressive behaviors. Individuals with this style
 tend to speak quickly and loudly, give direct eye contact, and
 display forms of power through their attire and by keeping
 physical distance.
A few benefits of this style in communication include
confident direction
 vr Assertively outlining a plan of action in the message
= V Energetically focusing on the end result and why you
 need to do as directed
You may also notice a few trouble spots:
_ v» Appears impatient, which interferes with establishing
 rapport
vr Seems overly critical, which interferes with mutual
 understanding
vw Displays aggressive behavior, which interferes with the
 audience’s feeling heard or supported
This style doesn’t work well when the audience or recipient of
 the message is looking for an expressive, warm, and facilita-
 tive communicator.
Spirited Style
The Spirited Style works best when the audience or recipient
 of the message enjoys spontaneity, enthusiastic brainstorm-
 ing, and emotional expressiveness. Individuals with this style
 tend to be animated, have a lot of voice inflection and display
 movement during interactions, and express views readily.

» Creative thinking with many ideas and turns of phrase
vr Spontaneously expressive, and uses warm, supportive
 language, which generates enthusiasm
ws Identifies how messages fit into a larger message or
 context
But take caution with the trouble areas:
= v» Energy and enthusiasm may overwhelm others, prevent-
 ing them from sharing their perspectives
vr Tends to avoid planning, details, and drilling down into
 the particulars of a situation
ww Seen as impulsive and disorganized, prompting the audi-
 ence to feel that the message isn’t clear
This type of person doesn’t work well when the audience
or recipient of the message wants organized and pragmatic
 information. Audiences or recipients of messages who need a
 planned approach to understanding the communication don’t
 work well with this style.
Systematic Style
When the audience or recipient of the message wants a
 detailed and thoroughly factual message is when this style
 hits a home run. Audiences who respond best with this style
 want an objective, methodical communication strategy.
 Individuals with this style tend to provide precise statements,
 brief comments with little emotional expression, little anima-
 tion, and keep physical distance.
Folks who favor this style display the following benefits in
 communication:
vr Thorough attention to process and details in giving the
 message and in the message itself
vr Factual and pragmatic, concise and precise messages
. v Careful, patient, reserved in delivering information

Considerate Style
People who display the Considerate Style interact best when

 friendly relationship work well with this style. Individuals with
 this style tend to talk slowly, use soft tones, and like close
 personal contact.

Do take time to heed the trouble areas of this communication

ws Creating a common understanding of the message being

 Systematic Style

 Style

Direct Style
The person with this style works best when followers need
 decisive direction and responds well to a fast-moving, aggres-
 sive leadership approach.

Ts are made up of people working collectively to solve
 problems, create new products, improve systems, and
 reach goals that can’t be achieved by one or two people alone.
 A team is more than a working discussion or problem-solving
 group. Teams go through stages of development and require
 the fulfillment of various roles and methods to produce synergy
 and collaborative efforts. In all phases of teaming, interacting
 with team members means that personality styles play a role
in how well the team really works together. Communicating,
 problem-solving, planning, managing expertise, and addressing
 conflict are a few of the processes of teams where the outcome
 is dramatically affected by personality styles.
Because teaming situations often require working extended
 periods of time with individuals across the organization,
 differences in perspective, strategy, and “how to get things
 done” are magnified by personality style differences. The
 team member who walks into the meeting room and immedi-
 ately puts an agenda on the wall is engaging differently from
 the team member who walks in, talks with everyone, and gives
 handshakes and back slaps while telling stories about last
 weekend’s game. Without understanding differences, these
 two could easily interfere with getting to the task at hand
 and create unnecessary conflict. You should know your team
38 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
member style and understand the different styles you're likely
 to work with. Knowing this information may enhance your
 effectiveness on teams.
There are numerous team models and theories you can
 research and read about. All these models, however, have
 four basic elements that are present in team interactions and
 processes:
vr Establishing a connection among team members so
 everyone is clear as to why they're members of the team
 or involved at a particular time in the process
vw Creating a common understanding of the goals, methods,
 and plans for the team to do its work
vw Supporting each other in fulfilling the mutually agreed on
 plan
vr Monitoring progress and re-evaluating future courses of
 _ action
As you engage in each of these elements of teaming, the use
 of your personality style reveals your team member style.
 Importantly, learning to flex your personality style enhances
 your team member effectiveness as you engage with team
 members through each element of teaming. Your team behav-
 ior combined with your personality style makes up your team
 member style.
All team member styles can be equally effective but not
 equally effective at all times. Team members need to flex their
 style to work closely with others and to address the demands
 of the team situation. You need to understand the benefits
 and potential challenges of each style and consider how to
 flex your style to work effectively with others.

a Team Member

 find the best solutions to challenges brought to the team.

Direct Style
The Direct Style works best when the team needs direction
 and team members want someone to take charge. This style
 says, “I know what needs to be done and here’s how we
 should do it!”
A few benefits of this style as a team member include
 vr Communicates assertively by asking difficult questions
and raising tough issues

vr Displaying assertive behaviors, which leaves some of the
 other team members feeling unsupported and discouraged
This style doesn’t work well when team members are cautious
 and like to stick with established, safe processes.
Spirited Style
The Spirited Style works best when team members are open
 to exploring new options and being spontaneous. This style
 says, “I have some great ideas. What if we . . . or considered...
 and maybe looked at . . ..”

 To fully understand time style, it’s important to learn how it

Your level of assertiveness and expressiveness affects how

 More assertive people tend to channel their energy into

All time management styles can be equally effective but not
in all situations. You may need to flex your style to complete

 each personality style.
Taking on the Direct Style
Feeling intimidated by the strong, forceful Direct Style person-
 ality? They aren’t as tough as they seem — just very focused.
To help your interactions go smoothly, keep in mind these
 tips when dealing with the Direct Style:
1. Focus on the person’s goals and objectives.
 2. Keep your relationship businesslike.
3. Be well organized.
4. Speak at a fast pace.
5. Ask direct questions.
80 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
Keeping Up with the
Spirited Style
 Have a co-worker who's full of energy and great ideas but
 hard to work with because, well, she’s full of energy and great
ideas?
Try some of the following tips:
1. Be entertaining.
2. Engage in brainstorming.
3. Allow her to share her ideas freely.
 4. Keep things moving.
5. Focus on inspiring ideas.
Cooperating with the
 Considerate Style
No one can be that nice — he must have ulterior motives,
 right? Nope, that’s just his Considerate Personality Style
 coming through. He really does want to help and support you,
 even at the expense of his own work. Go with it, but remem-
 ber to return the favor.
To help you get the most out of your interactions, here are
 some tips:
1. Focus on your relationship.
2. Be supportive of his feelings.
3. Make sure you understand his needs.
 4. Maintain a relaxed pace.
5. Give him time to build trust in you.
Chapter 11: Top Rules for Interacting With Each Style $&7
Engaging with a Systematic
 Style Person
When we say “just the facts, please,” we mean “just the facts,
 please.” A Systematic Style person doesn’t have time for idle
 chitchat or speculation; however, these detail-oriented people
 are an asset to any project or team.
To make the most of your interactions with the Systematic
 Style person, try the following tips:
1. Focus on facts, not opinions.
 2. Be thorough and organized.
 3. Avoid gimmicks.
4. Allow time for analysis.
5. Provide written evidence when possible.
8 2 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
Chapter 12
Top Ten Personalıty
 Style Tips
In This Chapter
» Paying attention to body language cues
+ Interpreting others’ actions
+ Appreciating the differences in people
+ Putting together a great team
P ersonality style is defined as the way people act when
 they're able to do things their own way. This doesn’t
mean that people act the same way all the time, but behavior
 is consistent to the point that it’s predictable. This chapter
 contains the top ten Personality Style tips that help you make
 the most out of your style and interactions with others.
No One Personality Style
 Is Better Than Another
Which personality style is best? That question may be one of
 the most frequently asked ones. The answer? In short, they all
 are. Each style has its own unique characteristics that in the
 right circumstance and at the right time come to the forefront.
 Check out these instances:
= 1 In a situation where immediate, decisive action is
 required, you'll appreciate the action-oriented Direct
 Style.
8 h Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
= vr When a spreadsheet needs checking for accuracy, you'd
 be wise to give this task to a person with the Systematic
 Style.
vr Need to rally the team around a new initiative? Well,
 that’s what people with the Spirited Style live for.
vr And if you have a problem and need to talk to someone
 who'll be patient and listen, you could do worse than
 X seek out someone with a Considerate Style.
Style Is Seen in Words, Tone of
 Voice, and Nonverbal Actions
It’s not just the words you use. People read into the sounds
 you make, whether harsh, pleasant, rapid, sarcastic, or what-
 ever. People read into your nonverbal actions — whether
 they're attentive, bored, or angry. Your expression and stance
 may show how you truly feel. The way you stand, shake
 hands, make eye contact, or not, all say just as much as the
 words you choose.
Make your words, tone of voice, and actions consistent in
 order to not confuse your message.
Knowing Your Style Helps Vou
 See How Others See Vou
SOMBER Understanding your style and how you come across to others
 & is an important step in developing stronger, more productive
 relationships. In fact, understanding how others see you, and
 learning to adapt according to their style, is one of the most
 proven ways to increase your influence and personal success
 in the workplace.
Why? Well, look at the core characteristics of your style (visit
 Chapters 1 and 2 for more info). Now put yourself in the shoes
 of a person with a different style. If you're a Systematic Style,
 you may prefer to review the pertinent information before
 making a decision. To someone with the Direct Style, who is
Chapter 12: Top Ten Personality Style Tips 8 5
oriented to take quick action, it may feel like you’re indecisive
 and hesitant — not the basis for a great working relationship!
Knowing this information, you could choose, say, to offer
 some preliminary thoughts on where you stand rather than
 waiting to pore over every last detail before making your deci-
 sion. By flexing your style, you meet the Direct Style’s prefer-
 ence for speed. Win-win!
Flexing Vour Style Takes
 Effort and Practice
In flexing your style, you need to adjust your behavior to
 achieve a desired result. If you don’t flex, you're likely to expe-
 rience frustration and disappointment in many situations. The
 folks around you may feel the same way as you.
While all four styles are unique, there are compatibilities
 between pairs of styles. Direct and Spirited people share the
 same preference for assertive behaviors, and Spirited and
 Considerate people share the same preference for expressive
 behaviors. So there’s a good foundation to work on because
 you only need to flex your expressive or assertive behaviors,
 but not both.
You need to work a bit harder to build a better connection
 with someone if you both share the style pairings of Direct/
 Considerate or Spirited/Systematic because you both need to
 flex your expressive and assertive behaviors, and this action
 requires more effort. It may be uncomfortable at first, kind of
 like writing with your opposite hand, but it gets easier with
 practice.
The Strengths of Each Style
 Can Be Carried to Extremes
Each personality style needs to learn how to limit the strengths
 of her style in order to make the style not become abusive.
 Extremes can be trouble spots and can become a problem.
8 6 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
Some of the major factors in taking your style behaviors to
 extremes include the following:
~V~ Stress
vr Being so extremely assertive (or not assertive) that you
 lack balance in influencing others
vr Being so expressive (or not expressive) that you lack
 balance in controlling your emotions
A strong emphasis on one style can mean a weakness in
 another. For example, a highly objective person may find
 himself neglecting people’s feelings.
Conflict Can Be Traced to
 Differences in Personality
 Styles
People get along with some folks more easily than they do
 with others. While there can be a variety of reasons in play,
 differences in personality style can often be at the root of the
 problem.
Take a quick personality style audit of people with whom you
 haven't established a strong connection but want to. Look for
 any obvious differences in style, and then learn how to flex
 your style to adjust your approach. Chapter 2 talks about flex-
 ing specifically.
Recognizing Styles Helps Vou
 Interpret Others’ Actions
Understanding the concepts of personal style and being able
 to identify others’ styles helps you to interpret their actions.
 For example, if Joe is generally friendly and outgoing, the fact
 that he gives you an enthusiastic hello shouldn’t be inter-
 preted as a sign of deep friendship. Joe probably gives an
 enthusiastic hello to most co-workers. If, on the other hand,
Chapter 12: Top Ten Personality Style Tips 8 7
MBER
 N
 &
Joe is a private person and gives you an enthusiastic hello,
 that signal may be taken correctly as a sign of friendship.
Knowledge of style sets up expectations of certain behaviors.
 When the unexpected occurs, you can more accurately attach
 meaning to it.
Differences of Style Should
 Be Appreciated
Sometimes you may forget to thank the Direct person for
 taking charge and initiating change or the Considerate person
 for having a calm demeanor when the argument seemed to be
 getting tense.
Take time to notice the differences you see in others, thank
 people for what they’ve said or done, and especially thank
 folks when what they have done is something that doesn’t
 come naturally for you or them.
Mixing Styles Can Compensate
 for Blind Spots on a Team
Competitive sports teams often comprise a high number of
 Direct personality styles, which makes sense when you think
 of the core characteristics of the style (for more on the Direct
 Style, see Chapters 1 and 2).
Work teams, though, benefit from having a greater range of
 styles. Diverse styles help the team compensate for possible
 blind spots. The careful Considerate serves as a buffer to the
 impatient Direct; Directs help push things through when the
 Systematic prefers one more look at things. Each style helps
 balance out the other.
When expanding or replacing a member of your team, it’s
 worth taking into account the spread of styles, and, if it makes
 sense to do so, consider people with styles that complement
 what you already have.
88 Personality Style For Dummies, HRDQ Special Edition
Choose Work That Suits Vour
 Personality Style
WNG/
If you find yourself having to flex your personality style too
 much or too often, you may be doing the “wrong” kind of work
 or be in a culture or environment that doesn’t suit you.
Look to your personality style for guidance as to the kind of
 work or environments in which you're likely to thrive. If you
 have a Systematic style and you prefer logical, straightfor-
 ward assignments where you can work alone, a career that
 offers this kind of work, such as Finance, would be a wise
 choice. Considerate people are good listeners and value
 personal relationships, and so they often choose careers in
 counseling or the caring professions.
